claims.text: Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion governs the strength and deformation or failure behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys.
Lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch impede dislocation motion.
Changing elemental composition can produce alloys with different degrees of atomic size mismatch.
Atomic size misfit induces lattice distortions and associated local stress fields.
Misfit-induced local stress fields affect dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Higher atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
Greater local lattice distortion hinders dislocation motion.
Hindered dislocation motion leads to higher yield strength.
Distortion fields can promote strain localization.
Strain localization affects ductility and toughness.
Relative to low-mismatch baseline alloys, alloys with greater atomic size mismatch should have higher yield strength.
Relative to low-mismatch baseline alloys, alloys with greater atomic size mismatch should show reduced dislocation mobility and more localized strain.
Minimal atomic size mismatch produces less pronounced lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism operates in single-phase, homogeneous concentrated alloys without second-phase segregation or significant short-range ordering.
Lattice distortion is expected to be less governing when other strengthening mechanisms, such as precipitation hardening, dominate.
Short-range ordering or electronic effects may influence the overall deformation behavior.
TEM can be used to assess dislocation density and patterns, while XRD can be used to assess lattice-parameter variations.
Failure to observe increased strength, altered dislocation behavior, or a correlation between distortion and mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.
